bases.stopping_rationale: The main article, including its participant-flow and result passages, was read and searched, and relevant protocol/SAP material was inspected. It describes missing follow-up as expected to be small and planned evaluation/sensitivity analyses, but no executed missing-outcome sensitivity result resolving this impact was located. The arm-specific incomplete-follow-up counts permit a calibrated probable judgment, while their timing, reasons and counterfactual event status remain unavailable.
bases.unresolved_premise: Whether missing outcomes, whatever their values, could make an important difference to the approved hazard ratio.

answers.justification: For the approved assignment comparison (randomized dapagliflozin 10 mg plus recommended therapy versus placebo plus recommended therapy), primary composite over follow-up (median 18.2 months), the flow diagram reports 14/2373 and 20/2371 with incomplete primary-outcome follow-up, plus 2 placebo participants of unknown vital status. The very small listed fractions and nearly balanced arm counts support that nearly all were followed; however these counts do not state timing, observed ascertainment for every composite component, or whether unobserved outcomes could materially alter HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85), so retain uncertainty. ITT membership is not itself proof of observation. Treatment discontinuation (249 vs 258) is not equivalent to missing outcome data.
unknowns: Timing and reasons for incomplete primary-composite follow-up and unknown vital status are not reported here.
Whether any participants' composite outcome was imputed is not established.
The missing-outcome pattern and its possible effect on the estimated hazard ratio are not quantified.

bases.source: Figure S2. Patient flow. Of 6,263 randomized participants, 3,131 were allocated to dapagliflozin and 3,132 to placebo. Dapagliflozin: 3,126 received allocated intervention and 5 did not; 444 discontinued intervention; incomplete follow-up for the primary endpoint was reported for 29; survival status was unknown for 2, including 2 lost to follow-up and 0 withdrawals of consent. Placebo: 3,127 received allocated intervention and 5 did not; 442 discontinued intervention; incomplete follow-up for the primary endpoint was reported for 23; survival status was unknown for 2, including 1 lost to follow-up and 1 withdrawal of consent.

Dapagliflozin was discontinued for reasons other
than death in 444 patients (14.2%), and placebo
was discontinued for reasons other than death
in 442 patients (14.1%). The vital status was
known at the end of the trial in all but 2 patients
in the dapagliflozin group and 2 patients in the
placebo group. The median duration of follow-
up was 2.3 years (interquartile range, 1.7 to 2.8).

counterevidence.implication: The flow chart does report some incomplete primary-endpoint follow-up (29 and 23), so the evidence supports near-complete rather than complete ascertainment.

answers.justification: The outcome-specific flow chart reports incomplete primary-endpoint follow-up for 29/3131 dapagliflozin participants and 23/3132 placebo participants, under 1% in either arm. It separately reports unknown survival status for two patients in each arm, and the main report confirms vital status was known at trial end for all but two per group. This supports outcome information for nearly all randomized participants, although follow-up was not complete for every participant.
unknowns: Reasons and timing for the 29 and 23 incomplete primary-endpoint follow-ups are not given here; the source also does not clarify whether unknown survival status counts overlap with those totals.

observations.text: DELIVER is a phase 3, international, multicenter, parallel-group randomized controlled trial; patients were assigned to dapagliflozin or matching placebo.
Primary outcome definition: worsening HF (unplanned hospitalization or urgent visit) or cardiovascular death.
All potential worsening HF events and deaths adjudicated by independent committee blinded to group assignment.
Primary composite assessed in time-to-event analysis using Cox model stratified by diabetes status.
Treatment stopped other than death in 444 (14.2%) and 442 (14.1%); vital status known at trial end for all but 2 in each arm; median follow-up 2.3 years.
Supplement clarifies urgent HF visit required IV therapy, analyzes time to first CV death or worsening HF, and states independent blinded adjudication.

approved_target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

measurement.method: Absolute change in HbA1c from post run-in baseline to week 24

reported_result.analysis_population: Modified intention-to-treat: randomized participants who received at least one dose of double-blind study drug and had baseline and at least one postbaseline assessment of any primary or secondary efficacy variable; missing values were handled using last observation carried forward.

bases.stopping_rationale: I inspected the primary article's HbA1c analysis and participant flow, the supplementary participant-flow figure, and the registry's HbA1c-specific outcome description and denominators. These Sources do not separate observed week-24 HbA1c from carried-forward values or state outcome-specific missing counts at that time point; therefore neither all/nearly-all availability nor materially incomplete availability can be established.
bases.unresolved_premise: Actual observed HbA1c measurements at week 24 and arm-specific imputed counts are not reported. The registry reports 221 placebo and 215 lixisenatide participants with baseline and at least one postbaseline HbA1c assessment during the on-treatment period, and says LOCF was used; these are analysis-eligibility counts, not counts with observed week-24 HbA1c. Completion of treatment (211 and 194) is also not outcome availability.

answers.justification: The outcome-specific registry passage gives 221/223 and 215/223 with at least one postbaseline HbA1c assessment, but explicitly applies LOCF and does not say how many had an observed week-24 value. Participants who stopped treatment and those whose measurements followed rescue were censored under the reported rules. Analysis denominators and treatment completion cannot substitute for actual outcome availability.
unknowns: Arm-specific number with an observed HbA1c at week 24.
Arm-specific number whose week-24 HbA1c was imputed using LOCF.

Twenty-nine (13%) lixisenatide-treated
participants and 12 (5%) placebo-treated
participants discontinued randomized
treatment, with the main reason being an
adverse event (8.5% for lixisenatide and

answers.justification: The protocol allowed rescue when glycemic thresholds were exceeded, including HbA1c above 9.0% through week 8 or above 8.5% thereafter, and measurements after rescue were excluded. Thus missing later HbA1c could depend on poor glycemic control. One participant in each group received rescue, but the report does not state which threshold triggered it, so this is a plausible rather than confirmed pathway.
unknowns: Whether either rescue event was triggered by HbA1c rather than fasting glucose.
How many additional week-24 HbA1c values were missing after treatment discontinuation and imputed.

bases.source: Supplementary Figure 2, Participant flow diagram. Of 1470 screened, 898 entered the 12-week run-in; 446 were randomized, 223 per group. Placebo group: 12 premature treatment discontinuations (5%): adverse events 9 (4%), other 3 (1%); 223 analyzed and 211 completed (95%). Lixisenatide group: 29 premature treatment discontinuations (13%): adverse events 19 (9%), protocol violation 2 (1%), other 8 (2%); 223 analyzed and 194 completed (87%). Figure footnote: numbers in parentheses are proportions versus the number randomized per group.

answers.justification: The flow figure reports premature treatment discontinuation in 29/223 (13%) with lixisenatide versus 12/223 (5%) with placebo; the article attributes most stops to adverse events and states that measurements after treatment cessation plus 14 days were excluded. The outcome used LOCF. Although the report does not tie most discontinuations directly to HbA1c, the differential stopping and censoring create a credible likelihood that missing week-24 values could differ from carried-forward values; the rescue rule also ties some censoring to glycemic thresholds.

observations.text: Centrally randomized 1:1 using treatment kit numbers and a centralized interactive voice response system; stratified by post run-in HbA1c and TZD use. Investigators lacked access to the randomization code.
Both groups used stepwise dose increase. Basal insulin adjustment was permitted in both arms; rescue short-acting insulin was permitted under stated glycemic thresholds.

Efficacy mITT required randomized participants to receive at least one dose and have baseline plus at least one postbaseline efficacy assessment; LOCF used. Twenty-nine lixisenatide and 12 placebo participants discontinued randomized treatment, mainly adverse events; one per group received rescue therapy.

Primary efficacy measure was absolute change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24. HbA1c decreased 0.7% versus 0.4%; LS mean difference about -0.3%, statistically significant. User-specified abstract estimate is -0.32%.

Sample size and ANCOVA specified; model included treatment, randomization strata, country, and baseline HbA1c. Article states sponsor representatives were responsible for design, protocol, SAP and analysis (page 6 lines 83-91); protocol/register/SAP comparison may be needed for selective reporting.
